_link.title: I can summarise the inputs, outputs and location of the stages of aerobic cellular respiration

toLevel2.stem: Where does glycolysis occur in the cell?

options.explanation: Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol, the fluid portion of the cytoplasm.
The cristae are the site of the electron transport chain, not glycolysis.
The matrix is where the Krebs cycle occurs, not glycolysis.
The nucleus contains genetic material; glycolysis occurs in the cytosol.

toLevel2.stem: What are the products of glycolysis?

options.explanation: Glycolysis breaks one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules and produces 2 ATP.
Carbon dioxide and large ATP yields are associated with later stages, not glycolysis.
Water is produced at the electron transport chain, and oxygen is an input, not a product of glycolysis.
Glucose is the input to glycolysis, not a product; pyruvate is the output.

toLevel2.stem: At which stage of aerobic respiration is oxygen used?

options.explanation: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the electron transport chain on the cristae.
Glycolysis does not require oxygen; it is an anaerobic process.
The Krebs cycle does not directly use oxygen, although it depends on the aerobic pathway.
Oxygen is specifically used at the electron transport chain, not at all three stages.

toLevel2.stem: Where does the Krebs cycle take place?

options.explanation: The Krebs cycle occurs in the matrix, the inner fluid-filled space of the mitochondrion.

options.text: In the cytosol of the cell
options.explanation: The cytosol is where glycolysis occurs, not the Krebs cycle.
The outer membrane is not the site of the Krebs cycle; it occurs in the matrix.
The nucleus contains DNA; the Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.

toLevel2.stem: How many ATP molecules are produced by the electron transport chain?

options.explanation: The electron transport chain generates the majority of ATP, producing 32–34 molecules.
2 ATP is the yield from glycolysis, not the electron transport chain.
4 ATP is not the standard yield for any single stage of aerobic respiration.
10 ATP is not the accepted yield of the electron transport chain.

toLevel2.stem: Glycolysis does not require oxygen to proceed.

options.explanation: Glycolysis is an anaerobic process that occurs in the cytosol without oxygen.
This statement is correct; glycolysis does not require oxygen.

toLevel2.stem: Carbon dioxide is produced during the electron transport chain.

options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is produced during the Krebs cycle, not the electron transport chain.
CO₂ is released during the Krebs cycle in the matrix; the electron transport chain produces water.

toLevel2.stem: During glycolysis, {{blank:1}} is broken down into two {{blank:2}} molecules in the cytosol.

options.explanation: Glucose is the starting substrate for glycolysis.
Pyruvate is the product of glycolysis, not the input.
Oxygen is not used in glycolysis; it is used in the electron transport chain.
Glycolysis converts one glucose into two pyruvate molecules.
Glucose is the input, not a product of glycolysis.
Water is produced at the electron transport chain, not during glycolysis.

toLevel2.stem: The electron transport chain occurs on the {{blank:1}} and uses {{blank:2}} as the final electron acceptor.

options.explanation: The cristae are the folded inner membranes of the mitochondrion where the ETC takes place.
The matrix is the site of the Krebs cycle, not the electron transport chain.
The cytosol is where glycolysis occurs, not the electron transport chain.
Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the chain and combines with hydrogen to form water.
Glucose is the initial substrate for respiration, not the final electron acceptor.
Carbon dioxide is a waste product of the Krebs cycle, not an electron acceptor.

toLevel2.stem: The Krebs cycle takes place in the {{blank:1}} and produces {{blank:2}} as a waste product.

options.explanation: The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.
The cristae host the electron transport chain, not the Krebs cycle.
The cytosol is the location of glycolysis, not the Krebs cycle.
CO₂ is released as pyruvate is broken down during the Krebs cycle.
Oxygen is consumed during respiration, not produced as a waste product.
Glucose is the starting substrate of respiration, not a waste product of the Krebs cycle.

toLevel3.stem: Why is glycolysis considered an anaerobic process even though it is part of aerobic respiration?

options.text: It does not use oxygen at any point during the reaction
options.explanation: Glycolysis proceeds without oxygen; it is the subsequent stages that require oxygen for aerobic respiration.

options.text: It produces oxygen as one of its main output products
options.explanation: Glycolysis does not produce oxygen; it breaks glucose into pyruvate and generates 2 ATP.

options.text: It only occurs when oxygen levels are extremely low in the cell
options.explanation: Glycolysis occurs regardless of oxygen availability; it is not triggered by low oxygen.

options.text: It takes place inside the mitochondria where there is no oxygen
options.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol, not inside the mitochondria.

toLevel3.stem: Why does the electron transport chain produce far more ATP than glycolysis or the Krebs cycle?

options.text: It uses the energy from electron carriers to drive a large proton gradient
options.explanation: The ETC harnesses energy from NADH and FADH₂ to pump protons, creating a gradient that drives ATP synthase to produce 32–34 ATP.

options.text: It directly breaks down glucose into individual carbon atoms for fuel
options.explanation: Glucose is broken down in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, not at the ETC.

options.text: It occurs in the cytosol where there is more space for the reactions
options.explanation: The ETC occurs on the cristae of the mitochondria, not in the cytosol.

options.text: It uses carbon dioxide as a fuel source to generate extra ATP molecules
options.explanation: CO₂ is a waste product released during the Krebs cycle; it is not used as fuel.

toLevel3.stem: What is the significance of the cristae being highly folded?

options.text: It increases the surface area available for the electron transport chain
options.explanation: The folded cristae provide more membrane surface for ETC complexes, maximising ATP production.

options.text: It traps oxygen inside the mitochondria to prevent it from escaping
options.explanation: The folds increase surface area for reactions; they do not trap oxygen.

options.text: It keeps glucose molecules stored within the mitochondrial membrane folds
options.explanation: Glucose does not enter the mitochondria; pyruvate does. The folds increase ETC surface area.

options.text: It prevents carbon dioxide from being released too quickly into the cell
options.explanation: CO₂ diffuses freely; the folds exist to increase the area for the electron transport chain.

toLevel3.stem: How does the location of each stage of aerobic respiration relate to the structure of the mitochondrion?

options.text: The Krebs cycle uses the matrix fluid while the ETC uses the inner membrane
options.explanation: The matrix provides the enzymes for the Krebs cycle, and the inner membrane (cristae) houses the ETC complexes.

options.text: All three stages occur on the outer membrane of the mitochondrion only
options.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol, and the other stages use the matrix and inner membrane.

options.text: Glycolysis occurs in the matrix while the ETC occurs in the cytosol nearby
options.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol, not the matrix; the ETC occurs on the cristae.

options.text: The Krebs cycle and ETC both occur in the same compartment of the organelle
options.explanation: They occur in different compartments: the Krebs cycle in the matrix and the ETC on the cristae.

toLevel3.stem: Why is water produced only at the electron transport chain and not at earlier stages?

options.text: Oxygen is only present at the ETC where it combines with hydrogen ions
options.explanation: Oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor at the ETC, combining with hydrogen ions to form water.

options.text: Water is actually produced at all three stages but in very small amounts
options.explanation: Water as a product of aerobic respiration is specifically formed at the ETC.

options.text: The matrix actively prevents water formation during the Krebs cycle steps
options.explanation: The matrix does not prevent water formation; the reaction conditions simply do not produce water there.

options.text: Glycolysis consumes all the water before it can accumulate in the cell
options.explanation: Glycolysis does not consume significant water; water production occurs at the ETC.

toLevel3.stem: A student says that the Krebs cycle produces most of the ATP in aerobic respiration. Why is this incorrect?

options.text: The Krebs cycle produces only 2 ATP; the ETC produces 32–34 ATP
options.explanation: The vast majority of ATP is generated by the electron transport chain, not the Krebs cycle.

options.text: The Krebs cycle does not produce any ATP at all during its reactions
options.explanation: The Krebs cycle does produce 2 ATP, but this is far less than the ETC.

options.text: The Krebs cycle only occurs in anaerobic conditions so it cannot make ATP
options.explanation: The Krebs cycle is part of aerobic respiration and does produce a small amount of ATP.

options.text: The Krebs cycle produces ATP but immediately uses it all for its own steps
options.explanation: The ATP produced by the Krebs cycle is available for cell use; the issue is that it produces far less than the ETC.

toLevel3.stem: The electron transport chain produces water because oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor.

options.explanation: Oxygen accepts electrons and combines with hydrogen ions at the end of the ETC to form water.
This statement is correct; oxygen is indeed the final electron acceptor and water is produced.

toLevel3.stem: The electron transport chain produces the most ATP because it harnesses energy from {{blank:1}} to create a {{blank:2}} across the inner membrane.

options.explanation: NADH and FADH₂ carry electrons to the ETC, providing the energy to pump protons.
Glucose is broken down in glycolysis; it does not directly fuel the ETC.
CO₂ is a waste product and does not provide energy for the ETC.
The proton gradient across the inner membrane drives ATP synthase to produce ATP.
There is no glucose reserve created at the ETC; the gradient involves protons.
Oxygen is used as an electron acceptor, not to form a barrier.

toLevel3.stem: Glycolysis is the only stage that occurs in the {{blank:1}}, making it accessible to cells that lack {{blank:2}}.

options.explanation: Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol, outside the mitochondria.
The matrix is inside the mitochondrion; glycolysis occurs in the cytosol.
The nucleus contains DNA; glycolysis occurs in the cytosol.
Cells without mitochondria can still perform glycolysis because it occurs in the cytosol.
Ribosomes are involved in protein synthesis, not cellular respiration.
Cell walls provide structural support and are unrelated to glycolysis.

toLevel3.stem: Carbon dioxide is released during the {{blank:1}} because pyruvate is broken down in the {{blank:2}} of the mitochondrion.

options.explanation: The Krebs cycle breaks down pyruvate derivatives, releasing CO₂ as a waste product.
The ETC produces water, not carbon dioxide.
Glycolysis produces pyruvate but does not release CO₂.
The Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.
The cristae host the electron transport chain, not the Krebs cycle.
The cytosol is where glycolysis occurs, not the Krebs cycle.

toLevel4.stem: A cell is treated with a drug that blocks the electron transport chain. Which products would still be produced?

options.text: Pyruvate from glycolysis and CO₂ from the Krebs cycle
options.explanation: Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle can initially continue producing pyruvate and CO₂, though they will slow without NAD⁺ regeneration.

options.text: Water from the ETC and large quantities of ATP from the cristae
options.explanation: The ETC is blocked, so water and the large ATP yield from the ETC would not be produced.

options.text: Only oxygen gas because the other pathways shut down completely
options.explanation: Oxygen is an input to the ETC, not a product; glycolysis can still proceed.

options.text: No products at all since all stages immediately stop without ETC
options.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol independently and can still produce pyruvate and 2 ATP.

toLevel4.stem: A scientist measures the ATP output of a cell and finds it produces only 4 ATP per glucose molecule. Which stages are most likely still functioning?

options.text: Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle only
options.explanation: Glycolysis produces 2 ATP and the Krebs cycle produces 2 ATP, totalling 4 ATP without the ETC.
The ETC alone produces 32–34 ATP, far more than 4 ATP.

options.text: All three stages are working normally
options.explanation: Normal aerobic respiration produces 36–38 ATP, not 4 ATP.
Glycolysis alone produces 2 ATP, not 4 ATP.

toLevel4.stem: During vigorous exercise, muscle cells may switch from aerobic to anaerobic respiration. Which stage of respiration continues in both pathways?

options.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and does not require oxygen, so it proceeds in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions.
The Krebs cycle requires products from aerobic pathways and slows without the ETC regenerating carriers.
The ETC requires oxygen and cannot function under anaerobic conditions.
Only glycolysis continues under anaerobic conditions; the Krebs cycle and ETC require oxygen.

toLevel4.stem: A researcher removes all oxygen from a sealed container holding living cells. Which change in waste products would be observed?

options.text: Water production stops because the ETC cannot function without oxygen
options.explanation: Without oxygen as the final electron acceptor, the ETC stops and water is no longer produced.

options.text: Carbon dioxide production stops because glycolysis requires atmospheric oxygen
options.explanation: Glycolysis does not require oxygen; CO₂ production from the Krebs cycle would slow but for a different reason.

options.text: ATP production increases because the cell compensates by speeding up all stages
options.explanation: Without oxygen, the ETC stops and total ATP production decreases dramatically.

options.text: Glucose production increases as the cell reverses the respiration pathway fully
options.explanation: Cells cannot reverse respiration to produce glucose; that requires photosynthesis.

toLevel4.stem: A student is asked to label a diagram of aerobic respiration. They place CO₂ production at the electron transport chain. What correction is needed?

options.text: CO₂ production should be placed at the Krebs cycle in the matrix
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is released during the Krebs cycle as pyruvate derivatives are broken down.

options.text: CO₂ production should be placed at glycolysis in the cytosol instead
options.explanation: Glycolysis does not produce CO₂; it converts glucose to pyruvate.

options.text: The label is correct because CO₂ is released at the electron transport chain
options.explanation: The ETC produces water, not CO₂; the label needs to be moved to the Krebs cycle.

options.text: CO₂ is produced equally at all three stages so no correction is needed
options.explanation: CO₂ is specifically produced at the Krebs cycle, not at all stages.

toLevel4.stem: Cyanide blocks the final enzyme in the electron transport chain. What would happen to ATP production in a cell exposed to cyanide?

options.text: ATP production would drop dramatically to only about 4 ATP per glucose
options.explanation: Without a functioning ETC, only glycolysis (2 ATP) and the Krebs cycle (2 ATP) can produce ATP.

options.text: ATP production would remain unchanged because other stages compensate fully
options.explanation: The other stages produce far less ATP and cannot compensate for the loss of 32–34 ATP from the ETC.

options.text: ATP production would increase as the cell redirects all energy to glycolysis
options.explanation: Even with increased glycolysis, the total ATP yield would still be dramatically lower.

options.text: ATP production would stop completely because all stages depend on the ETC directly
options.explanation: Glycolysis does not depend on the ETC and can still produce 2 ATP in the cytosol.

toLevel4.stem: A cell biologist detects high levels of CO₂ and low levels of water production in a cell. What does this suggest about the cell's respiration?

options.text: The Krebs cycle is active but the electron transport chain is impaired
options.explanation: CO₂ from the Krebs cycle is still produced, but low water output suggests the ETC is not functioning properly.

options.text: Glycolysis has stopped while the other two stages continue working normally
options.explanation: If glycolysis stopped, there would be no pyruvate to fuel the Krebs cycle.

options.text: The cell has switched entirely to photosynthesis instead of respiration now
options.explanation: Photosynthesis and respiration are separate processes; high CO₂ indicates active respiration.

options.text: All three stages are functioning at maximum capacity within this particular cell
options.explanation: If all stages were fully functional, water production from the ETC would also be high.

toLevel4.stem: If the electron transport chain is blocked, the cell can only produce {{blank:1}} ATP from glycolysis and {{blank:2}} ATP from the Krebs cycle.

options.explanation: Glycolysis produces a net yield of 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
34 ATP is the yield of the electron transport chain, not glycolysis.
Glycolysis does produce ATP; it yields 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
The Krebs cycle produces 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
32 ATP is associated with the electron transport chain, not the Krebs cycle.
10 ATP is not the standard yield of the Krebs cycle.

toLevel4.stem: During anaerobic conditions, {{blank:1}} still occurs in the cytosol but the {{blank:2}} and electron transport chain cannot proceed.

options.explanation: Glycolysis does not require oxygen and continues under anaerobic conditions.
The Krebs cycle depends on the aerobic pathway and slows without the ETC.
Oxidative phosphorylation requires oxygen and cannot proceed anaerobically.
The Krebs cycle requires NAD⁺ regenerated by the ETC, which needs oxygen.
Glycolysis is the stage that continues under anaerobic conditions.
Fermentation is the anaerobic alternative; it is the Krebs cycle that stops.

toLevel4.stem: A student detects CO₂ but no water being produced by a cell, indicating the {{blank:1}} is active while the {{blank:2}} is impaired.

options.explanation: The Krebs cycle produces CO₂ as pyruvate derivatives are broken down.
The ETC produces water, not CO₂; if it were active, water would be detected.
Glycolysis does not produce CO₂; it converts glucose to pyruvate.
The absence of water production indicates the ETC is not functioning.
CO₂ is being detected, indicating the Krebs cycle is active.
Glycolysis produces pyruvate, not water; its impairment would not explain the lack of water.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher compares ATP yield in cells with tightly packed cristae versus cells with few, loosely folded cristae. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text: Cells with tightly packed cristae produce more ATP via the ETC
options.explanation: More cristae surface area means more ETC complexes, allowing greater ATP production.

options.text: Cells with few cristae produce more ATP because there is less membrane resistance
options.explanation: Fewer cristae means less surface area for the ETC and lower ATP production.

options.text: Both cell types produce identical ATP because cristae structure is irrelevant
options.explanation: Cristae structure directly affects the surface area available for the ETC and therefore ATP yield.

options.text: Cells with few cristae compensate by increasing glycolysis to match the ATP output
options.explanation: Glycolysis produces only 2 ATP per glucose, which cannot compensate for reduced ETC capacity.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that removing the Krebs cycle would have no effect on total ATP yield because the ETC produces most of the ATP. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: Incorrect; the Krebs cycle supplies the electron carriers that fuel the ETC
options.explanation: Without the Krebs cycle, NADH and FADH₂ would not be produced, and the ETC would lack the electrons needed to generate ATP.

options.text: Correct; the ETC operates independently and does not need the Krebs cycle at all
options.explanation: The ETC depends on electron carriers produced by the Krebs cycle to function.

options.text: Incorrect; but only because the Krebs cycle produces more ATP than the ETC does
options.explanation: The Krebs cycle produces less ATP than the ETC, but it is essential for supplying electron carriers.

options.text: Correct; glycolysis alone can supply enough electrons for the ETC to function fully
options.explanation: Glycolysis produces some NADH but not enough to sustain the full output of the ETC.

toLevel5.stem: Heart muscle cells contain far more mitochondria than skin cells. What does this suggest about the metabolic demands of heart tissue?

options.text: Heart cells require more ATP from aerobic respiration due to constant contraction
options.explanation: The heart beats continuously and demands large amounts of ATP, requiring many mitochondria for aerobic respiration.

options.text: Heart cells use mitochondria for structural support rather than energy production
options.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, not structural elements.

options.text: Skin cells have higher energy demands but use anaerobic respiration exclusively
options.explanation: Skin cells have lower energy demands than heart cells and do not rely exclusively on anaerobic respiration.

options.text: Heart cells store excess glucose inside their mitochondria for future energy use
options.explanation: Mitochondria do not store glucose; they carry out respiration using pyruvate.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that aerobic respiration is 'better' than anaerobic respiration in all situations. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: Incorrect; anaerobic respiration provides rapid ATP when oxygen is unavailable
options.explanation: Anaerobic respiration is essential for short-term energy needs when oxygen supply is insufficient, such as during intense exercise.

options.text: Correct; aerobic respiration is always superior because it produces more ATP per glucose
options.explanation: While aerobic respiration is more efficient, anaerobic respiration is valuable when oxygen is unavailable.

options.text: Incorrect; anaerobic respiration actually produces more ATP than aerobic respiration does
options.explanation: Anaerobic respiration produces far less ATP; its advantage is speed and independence from oxygen.

options.text: Correct; cells should never use anaerobic respiration because it produces toxic waste only
options.explanation: Anaerobic respiration does produce lactic acid or ethanol, but these are manageable byproducts in short-term use.

toLevel5.stem: In an experiment, cells are given a radioactively labelled glucose molecule. At which stage would the labelled carbon atoms first appear as CO₂?

options.text: During the Krebs cycle when pyruvate derivatives are decarboxylated
options.explanation: Carbon atoms from glucose are incorporated into pyruvate, which is decarboxylated during the Krebs cycle, releasing labelled CO₂.

options.text: During glycolysis when glucose is first broken down in the cytosol
options.explanation: Glycolysis does not release CO₂; the carbon atoms remain in the pyruvate molecules.

options.text: During the ETC when oxygen combines with carbon to form CO₂ on the cristae
options.explanation: At the ETC, oxygen combines with hydrogen to form water, not with carbon to form CO₂.

options.text: Immediately upon entering the cell before any metabolic reactions begin
options.explanation: Glucose must be metabolised before its carbon atoms are released as CO₂.

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that organisms could survive with only the electron transport chain if given enough electron carriers directly. Evaluate this idea.

options.text: Theoretically possible for ATP production but cells also need the metabolic intermediates from earlier stages
options.explanation: The ETC could produce ATP with supplied carriers, but cells need intermediates from glycolysis and the Krebs cycle for biosynthesis.

options.text: Completely impossible because the ETC cannot produce ATP without glucose being present
options.explanation: The ETC uses electron carriers, not glucose directly; if carriers were supplied, ATP could be made.

options.text: Fully practical because the ETC is the only stage that matters for cell survival overall
options.explanation: Cells need metabolic intermediates from earlier stages for building molecules, not just ATP.

options.text: Impossible because the ETC requires carbon dioxide from the Krebs cycle to function
options.explanation: The ETC uses electron carriers, not CO₂; CO₂ is a waste product of the Krebs cycle.

toLevel5.stem: Two cell types have equal glucose supply. Cell type X has twice as many mitochondria as cell type Y. How would their ATP production compare under aerobic conditions?

options.text: Cell X would produce ATP faster due to greater mitochondrial capacity
options.explanation: More mitochondria provide more sites for the Krebs cycle and ETC, enabling faster ATP production.

options.text: Both would produce the same total ATP because glucose supply is the limiting factor
options.explanation: While total yield per glucose is fixed, the rate of production depends on mitochondrial number.

options.text: Cell Y would produce more ATP because fewer mitochondria means less energy wasted
options.explanation: Fewer mitochondria limit the rate of aerobic respiration; they do not increase efficiency.

options.text: Neither cell would benefit from extra mitochondria because glycolysis is the rate limit
options.explanation: The ETC is the major ATP-producing stage, so more mitochondria increase the rate of ATP production.

toLevel5.stem: A textbook states that aerobic respiration produces exactly 38 ATP per glucose. A student finds research suggesting the actual yield is 30–32 ATP. Which explanation best accounts for the discrepancy?

options.text: The theoretical maximum does not account for energy lost to proton leakage and transport costs
options.explanation: In practice, some energy from the proton gradient is lost to leakage and to transporting ATP out of the mitochondria.

options.text: The textbook is completely wrong and should be recalled by the publisher immediately
options.explanation: The textbook gives the theoretical maximum; the lower figure reflects real-world inefficiencies.

options.text: The research is flawed because ATP production is always exactly 38 in every living cell
options.explanation: Actual ATP yield varies and is lower than the theoretical maximum due to biological inefficiencies.

options.text: The student miscounted the ATP molecules during the experimental measurement in the lab
options.explanation: The discrepancy is well established in biochemistry and reflects genuine energy losses, not counting errors.

toLevel5.stem: Heart muscle cells contain many mitochondria because they require a high rate of {{blank:1}} to sustain continuous {{blank:2}}.

options.explanation: The constant energy demands of the heart require high rates of aerobic respiration.
The heart relies primarily on aerobic respiration for its sustained energy needs.
Heart cells do not carry out photosynthesis; they rely on aerobic respiration.
The heart contracts continuously, requiring a constant supply of ATP.
Heart muscle cells rarely divide; their high energy demand is for contraction.
While protein synthesis occurs, the primary energy demand is for contraction.

toLevel5.stem: The Krebs cycle is essential to the ETC because it generates the {{blank:1}} that carry electrons to the {{blank:2}}.

options.explanation: NADH and FADH₂ produced by the Krebs cycle deliver electrons to the ETC.
Glucose is broken down in glycolysis, not produced by the Krebs cycle.
Oxygen is consumed at the ETC; it is not generated by the Krebs cycle.
The ETC complexes are located on the inner membrane (cristae) of the mitochondrion.
The ETC is located on the inner membrane, not the outer membrane.
The ETC is located on the mitochondrial inner membrane, not the cell membrane.
